thread.title: Random Musings About A Foul Stock Market

author: Ray Merola
title: Random Musings About A Foul Stock Market
text:
Since early October, U.S. markets have taken a somewhat nasty turn down. Amidst the huffing and puffing by many market “experts” focused primarily upon the 24/7 news cycle, I offer you several general observations that have served me well over the past 35 years. I speak from the perspective of having seen several great bull and bear markets come and go.
courtesy of trophypartner.com
During the course of my investment lifetime, I've witnessed but one market with the potential to cause truly cataclysmic damages: the 2008-09 Great Recession market. At that time, there was a real possibility of a total, global financial collapse. Unlike other corrections/bear markets, the issues were of a structural, not cyclical. Financial liquidity dried up. The economy was like an engine trying to run with no oil in the crankcase. I believe we were on the precipice of another Great Depression.
Here's some good news....
Currently, I contend we are far from facing a structural 2008-09 financial meltdown. I contend we're into a more garden-variety correction/bear market triggered by certain geo-political events, Federal Reserve tightening, and the realization we're in a late phase, economic business cycle. Negatively-charged market sentiment has followed. The media's obsession with mixing politics and investing compounds matters.
Now some bad news....
If the current market correction shifts gears into true bear mode-- we ain't seen nothing yet. The S&P 500 ( SPY ) is down barely 10%. Indeed, if we head down a bear market path, then I harbor a specific concern: there are a whole bunch of young institutional money managers who've never been through a real bear market. Over the past 10 years, we've seen generally rising equity prices, tempered by occasional downdrafts. “Buy the dips” always worked.
These younger managers' perspective could color the depth of a real downturn. When the bear truly starts mauling all stocks indiscriminately; the quantitative analysis, algorithms, and textbook classroom theories go out the window. It's ugly and nothing seems to work. If that leads to full-on selling panic, we are in for a rough ride. Furthermore, there's another subset of other investors: yield-chasing, retiring Baby Boomers that collectively could accelerate damages. Some view the market as a source of ever-increasing incremental wealth and steady income, neglecting the hard lessons from the past.
However, for purposes of this article, let's presume market participants behave reasonably well. What might be some overarching principles to help get through a generally foul market?
Avoid Reacting To Headline News I don't mean stop reading them. Just don't accept headlines at face value. In particular, don't take their cue without additional due diligence. There is no substitute for hard work and critical thinking.
courtesy of the Baltimore Sun
Rarely are business headlines meant to provide actionable investment guidance. The objective is to attract you to read on – garnering clicks and eyeballs for the author / publisher. Good journalistic articles dissect the headline, and offers a full set of facts supporting it; then permit you, the reader or viewer, to draw a conclusion. These are few and far between. There's plenty of regular headline news competing for your attention: all at 100 decibels.
Hence, my second major point:
During times of market stress, the need to “do the homework” becomes even more important. If you elect to buy individual securities, it's imperative you understand each company like you are an owner. It's the time to roll up your sleeves and redouble efforts to understand the underlying business, and the corresponding stock. If you do not, it's like going to the casino. And at least at the casino, you might get a few free drinks. There's no free drinks on the Street.
Don't skim through headlines or accept others' analysis as-is; business men and women review multiple data points, analyze it, question it, think about it, then makes informed decisions.
Who's managing the company? What's your opinion of the management team, its strategies, and ability to keep investment promises? Have they navigated tough times before? As an investor, do you have confidence in the C-suite team?
Are the financials sound? Can the busines withstand an economic downturn? Are figures presented clearly? Do the financial "adjustments" make sense? Is forward guidance offered? Has it been accurate?
What's your own view of the overall newsfeed? Read past the headlines to delve into the details. Often, retail investors panic when they see their stocks going down, but really don't know why. Is it a broken stock or a broken company? Without doing the homework, it is nearly impossible to tell. Reading Street reports and listening to the experts won't get you through the woods.
What's your Fair Value Estimate for securities in your portfolio? Has the merchandise (the stock) been bid up too high, or is it selling at a discount?
Lastly, I offer the following counsel: DO NOT mix your politics with your investments. Whether you like or hate Trump, or a given political party is your business. I'm here to tell you if you try to make investment decisions based upon what you read in the funny papers about politics and politicians, you are very likely disarm chances of generating alpha. There's also a probability your political leanings will lead you astray when trying to perform objective financial analysis.
Unfortunately, I see many Seeking Alpha comment boards littered with all manner of nonsense about politics and politicians. Nearly all of it is worthless. Perhaps making such remarks may be some kind of catharsis for the commentator. The comments do nothing to enable superior investment returns.
Where Are We In the Economic Business Cycle? I am a proponent that economies run in cycles. Recessions give way to recoveries. Recoveries pick up steam as easy credit and robust demand permit businesses to expands until the economy begins to run “hot,” whereby reserve banks attempt to curb inflation (and associated hot air) by tightening credit / raising interest rates. Inevitably, economies peak and roll over into a new recession; and then the cycle begins all over again.
Historically, the full business cycle lasts about seven years. We've been in the current expansion phase for about ten years; therefore, we're running long, but coming out from a particularly deep hole. I submit we're into the late-phase of the cycle. During the late-phase, industrial and basic materials stocks peak, then begin to roll over. Bank lending reaches an apex, and bank stocks lose a key catalyst. “Full” employment reports make their way into the news. Wages improve as the markets for specific workers gets tight. The Fed embarks on a series of interest rate hikes to prevent the economy from overheating.
Presuming we're in a late-phase expansion, it's time to think ahead. I assure you Mr. Market is thinking ahead. He tends to look out six to twelve months into the future. When the late-cycle recovery gets long-in-the-tooth, money starts rotating into defensive stocks: healthcare, consumer staples, and utilities. Unfortunately, many of these names have already been bid up. I am constructive on Dominion Resources ( D ) and PPL Corp ( PPL ), but over the past several months these stocks have gone from good discounts to nearly Fair Value. Ditto Procter & Gamble ( PG ), a stock I sold recently specifically on valuation concerns.
Prepare A Shopping List Rather than worry and lament about the tape, I like to put together a “shopping list.” It's a kind of wish list of stocks I'd like to buy if I can get a big enough discount. Think of it like you're going to a store: some of the merchandise is overvalued, and some is discounted. However, during market sell-offs, more and more merchandise goes “on sale.” I love deals and discounts.
I've long tried to follow a “north star:” premier companies selling at a significant discount to Fair Value.
What makes a company premier?
There's a number of ways to determine it, but I stick with this mantra:
“Own the stocks of well-managed companies with a sound balance sheet, a strong franchise, that earn profits largely in cash, and are shareholder-friendly.”
Well-managed companies are marked by management teams that make promises to investors, then keep them. Of course, no one is perfect, and sometimes things happen to businesses that are out of its control. Therefore, if management must break a promise, company leadership explains why, and what they plan to do about it going forward. Good investors can discern management teams that drive the business, and those that make excuses. Well-managed companies set clear stratgies and objectives, then get results.
The best companies own strong balance sheets. The balance sheet is the bedrock of a good business. During times of stress, a strong balance sheet can enable a company to weather a storm; debt is manageable, working capital is positive, and liquidity is solid.
In addition, cash flow is better than net income. That's why I prefer companies that earn their profits in cash.
All this requires a second, most-critical analysis:
Does the stock trade below a reasonable Fair Value Estimate?
While the details are beyond the scope of this article, evaluating FVEs is just as important as identifying premier companies. Generally, the process of determining Fair Value requires a careful review of the historical valuation multiples of a stock, or DCF, then comparing it with recent prices. In a nutshell, it's a benchmarking exercise.
If I go to a store to buy a sweater, I must have some idea of the value of the sweater to know whether it's a real discount, or just a reduced price . My regular work on Seeking Alpha includes a FVE analysis for most of the stocks I cover.
A good shopping list identifies premier companies whereby the stock is selling at a significant discount to Fair Value.
Currently, my shopping list includes Bank of America ( BAC ), FedEx ( FDX ), CVS Health Corp ( CVS ), Celgene ( CELG ), Schlumberger ( SLB ), and AT&T ( T ). Royal Dutch Shell ( RDS.A ) ( RDS.B ) and Apple ( AAPL ) are starting to look interesting, too. The harder the market falls, the more stocks go "on sale."
Buy In Stages I like to buy securities in stages: never all at once. Going “all-in” at once is not only risky, but perhaps borderline arrogant. How can anyone know with complete certainty the top or bottom of a stock's price trajectory? No, it's best to scale in or out deliberately. Warren Buffett once quipped, “It's better to be partly right than completely wrong.”
I may leg into a new position via three to five tranches; over weeks, or even longer. As a long-term investor, I'm not interested in a quick pop, either. In most cases, I'm happier if a new stock position goes down : it provides me a chance to acquire more shares at an even better price. Defend your basis. Don't chase stocks up.
If you've done your homework, and believe your buying discounted merchandise (shares of stock) of a great business....after buying 100 shares at $20, why would you dislike the idea of buying more at $18?
Consider Reducing The Number Of Stocks I limit the number of stocks in my portfolio to ~15 core positions. As a retiree, on average I can spare ~15 hours a week on investment activities. I contend it takes at least one hour, per stock, per week for retail investors to really understand the underlying business, its financials, the management team, and follow the newsfeed. Spend less time at your own peril.
If you're working full-time, then for all but a few brave souls, I suspect a handful of stocks may be the limit.
Vince Lombardi, the late great Green Bay Packers football coach once said, “Fatigue makes cowards of us all.”
Trying to keep track of 30 stocks is paramount to running one's own mutual fund. It would be nearly a full-time job in itself. You will get tired. When times are good, we can be fooled into thinking we don't need to do the homework. Hey! Everything's just fine. However, when the bear comes to maul the portfolio, the need to understand these business, how it makes money, and how management is reacting to on-the-ground events becomes a requirement.
When investing, one of the worst feelings is watching your stocks go down and having no idea why.
Unfortunately, that feeling can lead to some serious errors in judgement; thereby turning a garden-variety market correction into a personal disaster. Don't sell low because the pain is too great. If you must sell low, sell because you believe the company, its management, or the business outlook is hopelessly broken.
Sell Some Losers During down markets, everyone hates to take losses. We like to capture the green on our winners, and wait for the losers to “get back to even.” That's a mug's game; a losing proposition. I try to think about each investment as, “Where is it going, not where it's been.”
Therefore, evaluating the business and a stocks' price versus Fair Value Estimate is be a forward-looking exercise. If you have a dud, get rid of it. Corrections and bear markets can last months. Who wants a portfolio where all the winners are harvested, and all that's left is a sea of red? Each position requires a cold-eyes review as to what are the businesses' and the stock's go-forward prospects. If there are better propositions out there, then sell, take the loss, and redeploy limited capital.
None of us get all our stock picks right. The great Peter Lynch once stated it only take getting two of three right to be a winning investor.
I also suggest avoiding the thinking, “It's not a loss until I sell it.” That sounds nice. It's comforting when sitting on losers. However, ask investors who went through the 2008-09 crash if they felt they didn't really have a portfolio loss because they hadn't sold the stocks yet. No...they had big, fat, ugly losses. There may be reasons for selling or not, but don't kid yourself into believing a 50% paper loss is not a real loss until you take it.
Final Thoughts Having invested over the years has taught me a few things. These include the value of hard work, patience, and flexibility. I've also seen some nasty market pullbacks, along with robust rallies.
Never panic. No one makes money while panicking.
During my investment lifetime, and effectively since WWII, the United States economy has been down, but never out. Steep declines have lead to even bolder upturns. I believe buying U.S. equities may be likened to taking a stake in the United States economy. The cycles run up and down. Some down cycles are painful. Nonetheless, great American businesses, whether run by youthful entrepreneurs or the most-experienced business moguls, always return to the top of the heap. I continue to be long America.
I hope to write you once more before we head into 2019. Merry Christmas!
Please do your own careful due diligence before making any investment decision. This article is not a recommendation to buy or sell any stock. Good luck with all your 2018 investments.
Disclosure: I am/we are long RDS.A, SLB, BAC, CVS, CELG, FDX, D, T. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions. I am not receiving compensation for it (other than from Seeking Alpha). I have no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in this article.
